    in the spec, not the catalogue: the service agent and its InferenceProvider association are at most DERIVED
    (E.1.3, E.1.4, E.10 item 3; D-621's cap rule), and no catalogue or corpus changes. Rejected for AU-RP-2: an aprov
    catalogue bump giving the service agent the class of its witness (every PROV digest of every new corpus moves, for
    a stronger claim than the cap rule allows).
  - **Why:** 0.2.0 is the version new imports and live captures will use; the recorded defects would give them wrong
    records (UC-2's gate recorder, UC-17..UC-22 in live capture), refuse runs (UC-16, UC-39..UC-41) or leave published
    figures inaccurate (the datasheet claims and counts), and none of the fixes changes a sealed corpus.
  - **Rejected:** keeping the record-only rule for 0.2.0 (the live-capture defects would reach the first live corpora);
    fixing only the live-capture and data-safety items (the user chose all); regenerating the sealed corpora (they are
    published and reproducible at their building commits; no sealed corpus holds a triggering input, per the 2026-11-01
    scan and each row's check).
- **D-1064 (2026-11-05, features known not to work on Windows are disabled with the reason; the user's decision of
  2026-11-05; core table, CLI refusals, `agentprov info`, tests and docs; the desktop app's half below; class 0).**
  The G5 clean-machine runs (D-867) found that live runs do not work on either Windows platform and that the job queue
  is POSIX-only, but the CLI let a Windows user start them: a run failed late (`worker_died` on x86_64, a failed build
  on ARM64) and `--queue-cpu` was refused with a message of its own. The user decided that these areas are disabled on
  Windows with an explanation of why, and that every message says where the feature works.
  - **Decision: one table.** `agentprov.platforms` (layer 0, standard library and `agentprov.errors` only, outside
    every stage scope) lists each feature, the platforms where it is unavailable (the operating system as
    `platform.system()` names it, and the architectures or all of them), the reason in plain words, where it works and
    the user-guide section. `unavailable(feature, system=None, machine=None, *, subject=None)` returns the entry or
    `None`; the system and machine are injectable for tests. On Windows the architecture is the interpreter's
    (`sysconfig.get_platform()`), because `platform.machine()` names the emulating host for an x64 Python on ARM64
    (D-867), and an emulated x64 interpreter builds x64 environments. Only tested and recorded limits are listed; a
    platform is never refused for being untested.
  - **Decision: the four limits.** (1) Live runs, on Windows x86_64 (the environment builds, but the worker exits at
    start-up for a reason not yet diagnosed) and Windows ARM64 (the AgentDojo backend cannot be installed: its pinned
    `cryptography` 50.0.2 and `cachebox` 5.2.3 publish no Windows ARM64 wheels, and backends install from wheels
    only), and any other Windows architecture; AgentDojo itself is tested upstream on Linux only. (2) `backends build`
    of `agentdojo`, `autodojo` and `agentdyn` on Windows ARM64 (the same wheels; a test reads the three locks and
    checks that the Inspect backend pins neither package, so its build is not refused). (3) `--containment
    sandbox-exec`, macOS only (it was refused off macOS already, by the probe's `not_applicable`; the message now gives
    the table's reason, and the refusal keeps its code `cli.refused.containment`). (4) The machine-wide job queue on
    Windows (`fcntl` locks).
  - **Decision: what is refused, and when.** Before any work starts, with exit 4 and the code
    `platform.unsupported`: every `agentprov run` mode that starts the backend worker (a run, `--preflight-only`,
    `--catalogue`, a `--dry-run` that plans cells, since the worker expands the plan, and `--tune-jobs`), checked before
    stdin, a key or the host probe is read; `agentprov estimate` inherits it, as it plans through `run --dry-run`;
    `backends build` and `--offline-check` of the three backends on Windows ARM64; `jobs start --queue-cpu` and `batch
    create` with a `queue_cpu` step (and the job manager itself, which the batch driver now treats as a permanent
    failure). Not refused: a host preset's dry run (the concurrency plan, computed in the CLI), `backends build
    --dry-run`, `info` and `--help`. `devrun` has no live mode; it already runs without the queue where the queue is
    unavailable. The message reads "<Feature> is/are available on macOS and Linux. On <platform> it is/they are not
    available yet: <reason>. See the user guide, <chapter, section> (docs/user-guide/<page>#<anchor>)."; for
    `sandbox-exec` it says "on macOS only" and has no "yet" (it is macOS's tool), and for the queue no "yet".
  - **Decision: `info` reports it.** `agentprov info --format json` gains the member `platform`: `system`,
    `machine` and `unavailable`, a list of the entries for this host (`feature`, `name`, `platform`, `works_on`,
    `reason`, `subjects`, `guide`, `message`). The text form gains a Platform section, and `info SOURCE --format
    json` (no host probe; the live-run form's call) carries the same member. No existing member is renamed,
    so the desktop app reads the same table to disable the same features with the same words.
  - **Docs.** User guide chapter 7 gains the section Platforms (the table), and its Containment and refusal tables
    name the new message; chapters 1, 8 and 10 say where each feature works and why it is unavailable on Windows (the
    ARM64 row of chapter 8 named `torch`; the locks show `cryptography` and `cachebox`); the packaged copy is synced and
    the CLI reference regenerated (`--queue-cpu`'s help).
  - **The desktop app (the GUI half, 2026-11-05).** The app reads the configured CLI's `info --format json` (S11: no
    import of `agentprov.platforms`, which the D-391 allowlist does not hold, and the checkout's CLI can be another
    install whose interpreter's architecture is the one that counts), once at start and after Settings › OK, in the
    background; until it answers, or for a CLI without the member, nothing is disabled and the CLI's refusal stands.
    Where a limit applies, the control stays where it is, disabled, with the table's message as its tooltip (shown
    although the control is disabled): Run Live… in the File menu (⌘L/Ctrl+L) and on Runs, Live Dev Run…, Run Live's
    Start… and Preflight Only…, Continue… of a New Job form whose command the CLI would refuse (`run`; `backends build`
    of the three backends on Windows ARM64, its `--dry-run` allowed), the job queue settings (Settings › Compute,
    Settings › Dev Runs' reservation) and `sandbox-exec` in Run Live's containment choice (shown disabled off macOS
    once the CLI has said so). Runs, Run Live, the job form and the queue settings show a notice ("Not available on
    <platform>", where it works and why, and a How to run it link to the guide section, on the Docs page or, from a
    dialog, in a guide window of its own). A job's queue reservation stays a recorded fact (no `--queue-cpu`) and a
    batch step gets no `queue_cpu` where the queue is refused. Rejected: hiding the controls (the user asked for them
    disabled with the reason); the app's own copy of the table (it can disagree with the CLI that runs the job).
  - **Rejected:** checking `os.name` or `sys.platform` at each command (several spellings of one fact, and no
    architecture); refusing whatever is untested on a platform (the user asked for the areas known not to work);
    refusing the preset dry run and `backends build --dry-run` (they start no worker, and the plan is useful before
    moving to another machine); a new refusal code for `sandbox-exec` (its `cli.refused.containment` is documented and
    unchanged); exit 5 `unsupported` (that code means the build lacks the capability; here the build has it and the
    platform cannot run it, a refused precondition).
- **D-1065 (2026-11-05, Check for Updates: a verified download and a one-click install the user confirms, never a
  silent self-replacement; the user's choice of 2026-11-05; CLI, settings, release workflow, tests and docs; class 0).**
  The desktop app and the command-line program had no way to learn of a new release, and installing one meant
  downloading a bundle by hand and checking `SHA256SUMS` in a terminal. The user chose "Check for Updates" with a
  verified one-click install and their confirmation. This decision is the CLI half; the GUI half (About, a Settings
  switch, a notice once per new version) follows and runs these commands as jobs (S11: the app keeps no network code).
  - **Decision: the check.** `agentprov update check --allow-network` (R2; exit 4 without the flag) makes one request,
    `GET https://api.github.com/repos/nickjones39/AgentPROV/releases?per_page=20`, through `raw.fetch`'s transport (TLS
    verified, no key or cookie, redirects only to an https host on the allow-list, which is `api.github.com` alone; the
    final URL is checked again), HTTP 200, at most 8 MiB, strict JSON (`agentprov.ingest`). The answer is untrusted: a
    release counts only with a tag `vX.Y.Z` and `draft` and `prerelease` both false; the highest version wins (not the
    newest date); an asset's address is built from the tag and its name (`https://github.com/<repo>/releases/download/
    <tag>/<name>`) and an answer that names another host or path is refused (`update.response.host`); names, sizes
    and the UTC `published_at` are checked; the notes become plain text, escaped (`escape_untrusted`) and cut at 8000
    characters. Versions compare in PEP 440 order for the subset the project uses (`X.Y.Z`, `aN`/`bN`/`rcN`, `.postN`,
    `.devN`, a `+local` label ignored); anything else is not comparable and never guessed (`null`). The document
    `agentprov-update-check/0.1`: `format`, `repository`, `checked_at` (UTC), `fetched`, `current` (`core`, `gui`),
    `latest`, `tag`, `update_available` (any known component behind; `null` when none is comparable), `behind`
    (`core`, `gui`), `published_at`, `release_url`, `notes`, `notes_truncated`, `platform`, `assets` (this platform's
    bundle: `name`, `size`, `url`), `checksum_asset`, `signature_asset`, `auto_check`, `check_due`. The app's version
    comes from `--gui-version`, or from `--bundle` where the bundle records it (macOS `Info.plist`).
  - **Decision: the daily check.** The answer is cached in `$AGENTPROV_HOME/update/check.json` (re-validated on
    reading; a damaged file is no check). `--if-stale` fetches only while the setting `update.auto_check` is not false
    (unset: on; the app's daily-check switch maps to it, the standing consent as `prices.auto_refresh` is for D-1062)
    and no check was made today in local time; otherwise it reports the cache (`fetched: false`) and says why.
    `agentprov update status` (R0) reads the cache only. The setting `update.last_notified` (`X.Y.Z`) holds the newest
    release the app has announced, so it tells once per version.
  - **Decision: what makes a download trusted.** `agentprov update download --allow-network` (R2) stages, in
    `$AGENTPROV_HOME/update/staging/<platform>/` (or `--dir`), in this order: `SHA256SUMS` (at most 1 MiB, strict:
    ASCII, `<sha256>  <name>` lines, LF, no name twice) and `SHA256SUMS.sig` when published; the signature, checked
    with `ssh-keygen -Y verify -f allowed_signers -I PRINCIPAL -n file -s SHA256SUMS.sig < SHA256SUMS` against the
    keys of the package's `agentprov/update/data/allowed_signers`; then the bundle (its size must be the listed one; at
    most 2 GiB; GitHub's asset hosts `objects.githubusercontent.com` and `release-assets.githubusercontent.com` are the
    only redirect targets besides `github.com`), whose sha256 must be the list's; then the archive's member checks
    (below). Any mismatch refuses (exit 1, `update.verify.*`, `update.archive`) and removes what was fetched. The rule:
    when the package lists a key, the release must publish a signature that verifies under one of them, or it is
    refused (`update.verify.unsigned`, `update.verify.signature`; without `ssh-keygen` exit 3); when it lists none,
    the files are checked against `SHA256SUMS` alone, which came over https from the same release, and the output says
    `"verification": "sha256"` and that this does not prove who published it. The package ships the file with no key
    yet; the maintainer adds one (below). The format and namespace are those of the v0.1.0 and v0.1.1 signatures.
  - **Decision: the extractor.** `agentprov.ingest`'s readers never write a member, drop file modes and reject links:
    right for evidence, wrong for an application, which needs its files on disk, a Linux bundle's executable bits and
    a macOS `.app`'s relative links. `agentprov.update.unpack` runs only on an archive whose sha256 was just checked and
    still treats it as untrusted: every name relative, `/`-separated, without `..`, a drive, a backslash, a control or
    Windows-reserved character, below the one expected folder (`AgentPROV.app` or `AgentPROV`), no name twice compared
    case-insensitively; only folders, regular files and (`.tar.gz`) symbolic links, no hard link, device or FIFO; no
    setuid, setgid or sticky bit (a file keeps only whether it is executable); at most 200,000 members and 4 GiB,
    counted while writing; files created with `O_EXCL` in a new folder, links made last (so nothing is written through
    one) and each resolved on disk (`realpath`, chains included) inside the bundle, or the folder is removed. The
    Windows `.zip` may hold no link. A `.dmg` is attached read-only (`hdiutil attach -readonly -nobrowse`) at a private
    mount point, its app checked by the same tree rules, copied with `ditto` (which keeps the code signature), checked
    again and the image detached. `tarfile` is used for its streams only (`extractfile`), never `extract`; SEC-11
    allowlists it with that reason.
  - **Decision: the install, per platform.** `agentprov update install --confirm --bundle PATH` (R2; exit 4 without
    `--confirm`) checks `--bundle` (the platform's folder name, its executable, not a link, a parent folder the user can
    write: an app run from the disk image is refused with "move it to Applications first"), verifies the staged files
    again (sha256 against `staged.json` and `SHA256SUMS`, and the signature rule), refuses a downgrade (exit 4), reports
    the same version as current, unpacks into `.AgentPROV-update/` beside the app (one file system, so the swap is a
    rename) and swaps: the app's folder becomes `.AgentPROV-previous/<name>` and the new one takes its place; an older
    previous version is set aside first and removed only after both renames, and a failed rename puts everything back.
    **macOS and Linux** (implemented): the swap is immediate (a running process keeps its open files) and the command
    says to quit and reopen the app now, since the running app is the old one and could load a file of the new one
    later. **Windows** (implemented): a running `.exe` and its folder cannot be renamed, so the new folder and a plan
    wait beside the app and a detached helper (`python -I -m agentprov.update.apply PLAN`, the CLI's own interpreter,
    no window) retries the two renames every 2 s until the app has quit, for at most 30 minutes, writing the outcome to
    `$AGENTPROV_HOME/update/applied.json`; the user reopens the app (left as an instruction). `agentprov update rollback
    --yes --bundle PATH` (R1) swaps the app with `.AgentPROV-previous` (one step; the version rolled back from takes its
    place), on Windows through the same helper. The install is recorded in `$AGENTPROV_HOME/update/installed.json`.
    Left as instructions: quitting and reopening the app. On macOS the files are written by the CLI, not a browser, so
    they should carry no quarantine attribute and the first-launch "Open Anyway" should not come back; this is not yet
    tested on a clean machine.
  - **Decision: package installs.** Without `--bundle`, `install` changes nothing: it names the command that upgrades
    the command-line program as it was installed: `uv tool upgrade agentprov` (a `uv-receipt.toml` in its prefix),
    `pipx upgrade agentprov`, `<its interpreter> -m pip install --upgrade agentprov`, or, for an editable install, "update
    the checkout with git, then `uv sync --frozen`".
    **Amended by D-1130 (2026-11-06):** a package install can also be upgraded by `agentprov` itself from the release's
    own verified wheels (`update download --package`, then `update install --package --confirm`: its own installer,
    `--no-deps --no-index`, never PyPI), a clean checkout on `main` by `update install --checkout --confirm
    --allow-network` (`git pull --ff-only` and `uv sync --frozen --group docs`), and the bundle is its own `agentprov`
    (`AgentPROV --cli`), updated with it; without a flag `install` still only prints the command, now with `automatic`.
  - **Decision: the release workflow.** `.github/workflows/release.yml` (manual dispatch with the tag and the id of the
    `bundles.yml` run at that tag) drafts the release. Its `assemble` job (contents and actions read) checks out the
    tag without credentials, checks the commit, takes the six bundles of that run, builds the sdists, wheels and source
    archive, and runs `tools/release_assets.py`: every `bundle-report.json` must say the build passed and name the
    tag's version (app and core), its commit with a clean tree and the package's sha256; `windows-amd64` is released
    as `windows-x64`; `SHA256SUMS` lists every file. Its `publish` job, the only one with contents write and in the
    environment `release` the maintainer approves, signs `SHA256SUMS` with the secret `RELEASE_SIGNING_KEY` when set
    (`ssh-keygen -Y sign -n file`, the key file under `umask 077` and removed), checks the signature against the tag's
    `allowed_signers`, fails when the package lists a key but the secret is missing, checks every file against the
    list, and creates a **draft**; the maintainer publishes it (nothing is published without the user's instruction).
    The private key never reaches the job that runs the builds.
  - **The one-time key setup (the maintainer's; no private key is generated or committed by a session).** (1) On your
    own machine, `ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C agentprov-release -N "" -f agentprov-release`. (2) In
    `nickjones39/AgentPROV`, Settings > Environments, create `release` with yourself as required reviewer and add the
    environment secret `RELEASE_SIGNING_KEY` with the contents of `agentprov-release`. (3) Add the line
    `agentprov-release namespaces="file" <the contents of agentprov-release.pub>` to
    `src/agentprov/update/data/allowed_signers` and commit it; it ships with the next release, from which every update
    must be signed. Your personal key, which signed v0.1.0 and v0.1.1, may be listed too (principal
    `58574515+nickjones39@users.noreply.github.com`), so a release signed by hand also verifies. (4) Keep the private
    key offline or delete it; a lost or exposed key is replaced by repeating (1) to (3) and removing the old line.
  - **Rejected:** a silent or automatic install (the user's choice: every install is confirmed, and the app never
    replaces itself unasked); GitHub's `/releases/latest` (one release chosen by GitHub's flag and date, so the
    pre-release and order rules could not be the client's own); trusting `browser_download_url` (an answer could point
    a download anywhere); a signing library (minisign, PyNaCl, `cryptography`: a new dependency) or GPG (not on macOS or
    Windows by default); Sigstore (verification needs either the network to its services or a library); checksums
    alone once a key exists (the list comes from the same place as the file it vouches for); the ingest readers for
    the install (they write nothing, drop modes and reject links, by design); overwriting the bundle's files in place
    (a failure mid-way leaves a mixed app, and there is no previous version to go back to); a swap on the next launch
    inside the app (code in the GUI before Qt starts, which this half leaves to the GUI; the helper keeps the swap in
    the CLI); Windows' replace-at-reboot (`MoveFileEx` delayed: a reboot, and administrator rights for some folders);
    upgrading the pip or uv install itself (the package manager owns that environment, and a program upgrading the
    environment it runs from can break mid-way; **reversed by D-1130** for the release's own verified wheels, installed
    by that package manager with no resolver and no index, after the user's confirmation); a network call in the app (S11).
  - **Downstream effects.** No AER, SEM, PROV, corpus or manifest bytes change and no stage digest moves (`update/`,
    `cli/`, `jobs/tiers.py` and `settings.py` are outside every stage scope). New: the component `update` at layer 2
    (it imports `raw.fetch`, `ingest`, `io`, `settings`), three SEC-11 process starters (`ssh-keygen`; `hdiutil` and
    `ditto`; the Windows helper) and the `tarfile` allowance; spec N.2.17's row; tiers (`update status` R0; `update
    check`, `update download`, `update install` R2; `update rollback` R1). The GUI's forward parity (D-654) needs forms
    or exclusions for the five subcommands and their flags, and the GUI half consumes `agentprov-update-check/0.1`.
    `bundles.yml` is unchanged; the release plan's manual `SHA256SUMS` steps can use `release.yml`.
  - **Tests:** `tests/update/test_update_releases.py` (version order, platforms, newer/same/older, pre-releases and
    drafts ignored, malformed, oversized and other-host answers refused, the redirect allow-list, notes, the cache and
    the local day), `tests/update/test_update_verify_unpack.py` (`SHA256SUMS`, the key rule, a real `ssh-keygen`
    signature good and bad, hostile tar and zip members, escaping links, setuid, the disk image),
    `tests/update/test_update_cmd.py` (check, status, `--if-stale` and the setting, download good and refused, install
    and rollback on simulated macOS, Linux and Windows bundles, the Windows helper's retries and timeout, package
    installs), `tests/repo/test_release_workflow.py`, `tests/jobs/test_jobs.py` (tiers),
    `tests/cli/test_cli_contract.py` (the command set).
  - **The GUI half (2026-11-05; class 0).** The app runs these commands with its configured CLI in the pool
    (`gui/src/agentprov_gui/updates.py` builds the argv and reads the documents defensively; `ui/updates.py` holds one
    `UpdateController` per main window, so a download goes on when About closes). About gains an Updates section: the
    last check from `update status` (no network), the newest release and its notes as plain text (S1), **Check for
    Updates** (`update check --allow-network --bundle APP --gui-version V`; Help › Check for Updates… opens About and
    checks), **Download and Install…** (`update download`, then a confirmation naming the folder replaced, the version,
    the verification and the `.AgentPROV-previous` rollback, then `update install --confirm --bundle APP`; the
    "SHA256SUMS only, does not prove who published it" note when no key is listed; the CLI's quit-and-reopen or, on
    Windows, applied-after-quit lines; after an install the button stays off until the app starts again, since a
    second install from the old running app would replace the version kept for rollback), and the terminal command of
    each action. `--bundle` is the frozen app's own
    folder; an app that is not a bundle shows **Show the Upgrade Command** (`update install` without `--bundle`) and
    installs nothing. At start-up, unless `update.auto_check` is false, `update check --if-stale` runs in the
    background (silent when offline or without a CLI); a newer release that differs from `update.last_notified` gets
    one notice (Update Now: About's flow; Later: asked again next start; Skip This Version: `settings set
    update.last_notified X.Y.Z`). Settings › Updates is the `update.auto_check` switch. No platform limit (D-1064)
    covers updates; a CLI refusal is shown as its reason. Forward parity: forms for the five subcommands (not in the
    New Job menu), `update install --confirm` managed (after the confirmation), `update rollback --yes` excluded (no
    rollback button; the install's result shows the command). Rejected: a job per command in Runs (a check or a
    notice would fill the job list; the long download runs with its own four-hour bound instead), announcing a cached
    answer while the daily check is off, and setting `update.last_notified` when the notice is merely shown (Later
    asks again, as the user chose). Tests: `gui/tests/test_updates.py` (fake CLI answers: commands, parsing, hostile
    notes, the confirmed, declined and refused installs, Windows, a package install, the start-up rules, the notice,
    the setting), the forward and reverse parity and tooltip walks.
- **D-1066 (2026-11-05, sealed corpora are read-only; the user's yes of 2026-11-05; class 0).** macOS Finder wrote 53
  `.DS_Store` files into sealed corpora, and `verify --level chain` then failed on every one of them with
  `corpus.tree.stray`.
  - **Decision: seal read-only.** After the swap, `package` (a fresh or a resumed seal) clears the write bits of every
    file and directory of the sealed tree (`agentprov.corpus.protect`: `protect`, `lift`, `is_protected`). Directories
    go bottom-up and DIR last. On Windows only files get the read-only attribute. Files that already have no write bit,
    such as raw objects, are left as they are. A refused protection is a notice; the seal still succeeds.
  - **Decision: removal and output.** `io.remove.rmtree` gives the write bit back to a read-only directory inside the
    tree it removes. It never changes a file's mode or a directory above the tree. The pre-check's sealed-copy cleanup
    uses it. No command writes into a sealed tree; `derive`/`recompute --out`, `verify --level rederive` and
    `package --deposit` write new, writable files.
  - **Decision: stray detail.** The `corpus.tree.stray` detail for an operating-system metadata file (`.DS_Store`,
    `._*`, `Thumbs.db`, `desktop.ini`) says what wrote it and gives the `find -delete` cleanup. Its code and severity
    are unchanged.
  - **Decision: corpora sealed before 0.2.0.** Their write bits are cleared by hand (`chmod -R a-w`) once the
    2026-11-05 chain re-verification is clean; no byte of any corpus changes. To change a sealed tree, run
    `chmod -R u+w DIR` first (user guide chapter 5, H.1.5(3)).
  - **Why:** a sealed corpus is a published, hash-chained artefact. A stray file breaks its verification without
    changing any record, and file-system protection stops the common writers (Finder, editors, a mistaken `cp`).
  - **Rejected:** a verify that ignores operating-system metadata files (it weakens the closed-tree check that finds
    real tampering); macOS-only measures such as `.metadata_never_index` or `chflags uchg` (not portable, and `uchg`
    blocks `rmtree` and the Trash); leaving it to the guide alone (the files had already been written).
- **D-1067 (2026-11-05, a LAN model server stays class `api`; the user's choice of 2026-11-05 on AU-RN-8; amends D-721
  and N.2.1b item 3a; class 0).** D-721 said a keyless LAN model server (`--allow-lan-endpoint`, D-698) would count as
  `local` once the egress proxy forwards LAN traffic. The forward mode landed on 2026-10-22 (D-664), but the CLI kept
  classing it `api`, and Run Live followed the entry's `local` flag: it hid the caps and passed
  `--i-consent-to-local-run`, so its command for a LAN server was always refused (`cli.refused.api_caps`, exit 4).
  - **Decision: the rule.** `local` stays a `local = true` entry whose resolved base URL is on loopback. A LAN server is
    `api`: API consent (the prompt or `--i-consent-to-api-costs`; `--i-consent-to-local-run` is refused) and all four
    caps (`--max-calls`, `--max-cost-usd`, `--price-in`, `--price-out`; prices of 0 are allowed for a server that bills
    nothing). Nothing else about the LAN path changes: keyless, literal private addresses only, the opt-in per run,
    the egress proxy's forward mode under `sandbox-exec`.
  - **Decision: the CLI says why.** The refusals and the class notice name the LAN case ("a LAN model server is an API
    endpoint: prompts and replies leave this machine"), the consent text says the data leaves the machine, and the
    `--allow-lan-endpoint` help says the caps and API consent apply (`agentprov.cli.live.policy.api_reason`,
    `is_lan_base_url`).
  - **Decision: Run Live.** It shows the caps and asks for API consent when *Allow a LAN model server* is ticked or a
    local entry's base URL is off loopback, as the CLI classes the run. The opt-in alone is enough because the app
    cannot see a base URL stored in the settings (D-699) or `.env`; with a loopback base URL the CLI still classes the
    run `local`, and it accepts the caps and `--i-consent-to-api-costs` there too.
  - **Why:** the caps and the API consent exist because prompts and replies leave the machine, not only because a
    provider bills. A LAN server is another computer, reached over plain `http` across the network (G.9.2), so the
    operator should consent to that as for an API, and the caps still bound how many calls the run makes.
  - **Rejected:** classing a LAN server as `local`, as D-721 planned (the local consent and optional caps would let
    a run send its data off the machine without the API consent); a third class `lan` (a new value of
    `live.endpoint_class` and of the GUI's choices for the same consent and caps as `api`).
- **D-1068 (2026-11-05, the class-1 items of the 2026-11-05 pipeline-performance review; the user's yes of 2026-11-05;
  class 1).** The review (profiles of `validate --corpus`, `recompute` and `verify` on sealed corpora, M5 Ultra) found
  that, after the tier-4 round trip (81–89 % of post-AER CPU, not addressed: P9 below), worker churn was the largest
  cost: each T1 start took 1.3–2.4 s of wall time and about 1.2 CPU-s, of which 0.74 s loaded all 68 semantics
  profiles and 0.60 s computed the D-550 cache context with three walks of the whole package, and every worker retired
  at the end of each `WorkerPool.run`, so a 3,232-execution re-map started 158 workers and a warm `validate --corpus`
  105 (about two thirds of its 194 CPU-s). No output byte changes; only code digests move (regen-batch row 187).
  - **Decision P1: workers outlive a batch.** At the end of a batch a worker that may still serve jobs is parked and
    the next batch of the same pool takes it (G.4.7 as built). It keeps its process, limits, audit hook and job count;
    only module-level caches cross batches, which G.4.7 already requires to be pure. Memory stays bounded by the D-554
    rule: a worker is parked only while its lifetime peak is at most `ADMISSION_RETIRE_PEAK` (512 MiB, by the kernel's
    lifetime maximum where the host has one, never below the watchdog's largest per-job peak), it has served fewer
    than `jobs_per_worker` jobs, the pool is open and fewer than the pool's worker count are parked. `close()`, a
    `with` block, the pool's collection (a `weakref.finalize` over the parked list, which holds no reference to the
    pool; the batch spool no longer holds one either) or the interpreter's exit stops them. The importer, `validate
    --corpus`, the migration gate and the withhold scan close their pools.
  - **Decision P2: a worker loads what its jobs name.** The pool derives a batch's preload from its jobs' params (the
    refs of `semantics` that match the profile-reference grammar, at most 64, and whether any carries `fidelity`) and
    passes it on the argv (`--preload-semantics`, `--preload-fidelity`; G.4.2 as built). The worker sets it before it
    imports the job table, the `prov` and `validate` job modules load exactly those shipped profiles and compute the
    cache context only when asked, and the audit hook follows (G.4.4). A job is sent only to a worker whose preload
    covers it; otherwise that worker is retired and one is started with the batch's preload. A process given no
    preload (the host probe, the `--in-process` parent, the migration gate's workers) loads everything, as before.
    The cache context needs one walk of a closure instead of three of the package (P5).
  - **Decision P5: the D-550 context's code part is an import closure.** `validate/cache.py` derives, with `ast` in
    each process, the files the import closure of `validate.prov` and `validate.cache` reaches (absolute, relative,
    lazy and `TYPE_CHECKING` imports, literal `import_module` calls, the enclosing package `__init__.py` files) and
    hashes them; the context keeps the library digests, the Python build, the options and the vocabulary version
    (format `agentprov-tier4-cache/2`; entries of `/1` are misses and age out). An edit inside the closure is a miss,
    an edit outside it (the CLI, the importer, an adapter) is not; a test pins both and an independent walk. Release
    mode never serves an entry: `derive`/`recompute` of a release-mode corpus now open the cache in audit mode, as
    `validate --release` and `verify --release` did.
  - **Decision P7: no fsync for trees that are removed.** `RawObjectStore(durable=False)` skips the `fsync` of a new
    object and of its shard directory, nothing else (G.3.1 as built). The T1 input stores of `import`, `validate
    --corpus`, the withhold scan and the migration gate use it; `recompute`/`derive` create the stores of their T1
    inputs after the output writer is open, inside `transient_stores()`, so `NEW`'s own store stays durable while a
    dry run's whole private tree and `verify`'s trees are transient. A staged `validate` input is removed with one
    `unlink` per name (it was a `chmod` and an `unlink`).
  - **Approved separately (class 0, with P3 and P4):** P3 (parallel, fd-cached `verify --level chain`), P4 (`rederive
    --sample` limited to the sample's raw closure), P8 (streaming the index and register in the `validate` and
    `verify` parents), R7 and R8 (removals). They are another change set of the same batch.
  - **Why:** the costs were measured, not assumed; each change keeps outputs byte-identical across runs, processes and
    worker counts (the K RPR-8 tests, the golden, gate-D and compat gates and the C.16 vectors are unchanged), and a
    scratch corpus built at the parent commit recomputes at this one with only the explained code-digest drift.
    Measured on the sealed `ast-survey-agentdojo-rg2` (3,232 executions, `--jobs 8`, through the queue, shared load;
    CPU-s = user + sys of the command and its workers, parent commit → this change): `validate --corpus` cold
    1,384 → 1,314 (−5 %), warm 208 → 151 (−27 %; worker starts 105 → 56, the rest being G.4.7's 64-job recycling),
    `recompute --dry-run` 1,634 → 1,291 (−21 %; wall 257 → 205 s), with identical reports and counters.
  - **Deferred:** P6, validating each AER once and off the parent (the parent validates each AER up to three times in a
    re-map and loads each twice: 20–28 ms of serial CPU per execution, which caps scaling at 16–22 busy workers); it
    changes where the write gate's input is checked, so it needs a design note before code.
  - **Rejected:** P9, a local override of the `prov` package's encoder for the round trip (two encodes are 47–52 % of
    tier 4): D-555 keeps the round trip on the published library, and a local copy would test our encoder rather than
    the library's reading of our document; a hand-kept module list for the cache context (it drifts, and an
    under-keyed context serves stale outcomes); a pool-level opt-in for P1 (every pool runs several batches, and the
    bound is the same D-554 rule); a lazy profile load after the audit hook (G.4.4 loads before the hook).
  - **Kept:** R1–R6 of the review's removal list (the old-format readers, the D-31 archives, the migration gates). They
    look unused from the current pipeline, but stored and sealed corpora still record the old formats and versions,
    and the gates are the regression evidence of the migration.
- **D-1069 (2026-11-05, `validate --corpus` accounts for the raw objects a sealed corpus version withholds: the AER
  checks that need their bytes are skipped, not `aer.blob.missing`; the 2026-11-05 profiling finding, investigated and
  fixed with the user's approval; `corpus/validation.py`, tests and docs; class 0).** Object-level withholding (H.4.5
  item 2; D-231, D-232) keeps an execution released while the bytes of a raw object it cites leave `raw/objects/` at
  sealing (into the private sidecar). `verify --level chain` accounts for such an object (`raw_withheld`, "withheld,
  never missing"), and `recompute`/`rederive` call the executions that need it `unverified` (H.4.5(6); BF-20, CB-6).
  `validate --corpus` handed the AER validator the sealed raw store with no knowledge of `WITHHELD.json`, so every
  locator or artefact check that needed a withheld object failed with `aer.blob.missing`, and in dev mode every such
  execution failed: all 1,055 of `ast-survey-agentharm-rg2`, all 1,747 of `fragfuse-agentharm-w2` (each execution
  cites its log archive's withheld `header.json` member) and 6 of a 500-execution sample of `dtap-bench-w2c` (a
  `config.yaml` withheld by `dtap-bench@3:email-withheld`). The sealed `validation/results.jsonl` rows pass, because the
  importer validated before sealing withheld the bytes; no code change since sealing is involved.
  - **Decision.** In corpus mode, a sealed corpus's `WITHHELD.json` (read with `decode_withheld`) names the objects the
    version withholds. An `aer.blob.missing` error whose header artefact, locator or `$blob` names one of them is
    replaced by the AER skip "raw-store checks (V20, V21): a raw object this corpus version withholds (WITHHELD.json)":
    the check cannot run, so it is neither passed nor failed (N.2.5's "skipped, never passed"). The row passes in dev
    mode; under `--strict` and `--release` the skip fails it, as every skip does (D8). Such a row is not compared with
    its stored row (`results_not_compared`, never `validate.results.differ`), since that row was made with the bytes
    present. The counter `aer_withheld` and one notice give the number. Every other finding stays; an absent object the
    ledger does not list, or a `WITHHELD.json` that does not decode (with a notice), stays `aer.blob.missing` (fail
    closed). The ledger itself is `verify --level chain`'s to check.
  - **Digest effect:** none. `corpus/validation.py` is outside every stage scope; the importer's and `derive`'s
    validation stage (which runs before sealing, with the bytes present) is unchanged, so no AER, SEM, PROV or
    validation digest moves and no corpus changes. Only the read-only `validate --corpus` report of a sealed corpus that
    withholds objects cited by released executions changes.
  - **Rejected:** teaching `AerValidator` or `LocatorResolver` about withheld objects (class 1 for every family, for a
    sealed-corpus concern the corpus layer owns); passing the check as `pass` (a check that did not run never passes);
    leaving it a failure with a better message (the corpus is as sealing made it, and `verify` already accepts it);
    accepting any absent object in a sealed corpus (it would hide a deleted object, the SEC-15 row).
- **D-1070 (2026-11-06, the update notice tells an out-of-date `agentprov` program apart from an out-of-date app:
  only then is the app's bundle offered; the user's report and yes of 2026-11-06; GUI `updates.py`, `ui/updates.py`,
  tests and docs; class 0).** The desktop app runs the `agentprov` program of the configured checkout or package
  install (Settings › General), and `update check` compares both it (`behind.core`) and the app (`behind.gui`) with the
  newest release (D-1065); `update_available` is true when either is behind. The app read only `update_available`, so
  a current app whose program was older announced "AgentPROV X.Y.Z is available" at every start and offered Update
  Now, which downloads and installs the bundle: that cannot change the program, so the notice came back at the next
  start. It happened on the maintainer's machine after the 0.2.0 release: the installed 0.2.0 app ran the main
  checkout's `.venv`, whose editable install still carried the 0.1.1 metadata (`core` 0.1.1, `gui` 0.2.0).
  - **Decision.** The app reads `behind` (`Check.behind_core`, `Check.behind_gui`; a value that is not a boolean is
    unknown). When `behind.core` is true and `behind.gui` is not (`Check.cli_only`), only the program is out of date:
    the start-up notice is titled "The agentprov this app runs is out of date", names the app's version (current), the
    program's and the newest release, says that updating the app would not change the program and that Settings ›
    General names it, and its primary button is **Show the Upgrade Command**. About's button becomes Show the Upgrade
    Command too, and both run `agentprov update install --format json` without `--bundle` (D-1065's path for an app
    that is not a bundle), which prints that program's upgrade command (`git pull`, then `uv sync --frozen` for a
    checkout; `uv tool upgrade`, `pipx upgrade` or `pip install --upgrade` for a package install) for the user to
    run. Nothing is downloaded or installed in that case. **Amended by D-1130 (2026-11-06):** the button is now
    **Update agentprov…**: after the user's confirmation it updates that program itself when it can (a package install
    from the release's verified wheels, a clean checkout on `main` by fast-forward) and otherwise shows the command as
    before; the app itself is still not downloaded or replaced. When the app is behind, whatever the program, nothing
    changes: Update Now and Download and Install… as before. The notice is still shown once per release, and Skip This
    Version still records it. A CLI whose document has no `behind` gives the old behaviour.
  - **Digest effect:** none. The GUI is outside every stage scope and the CLI is unchanged; no corpus, AER, SEM, PROV
    or validation digest moves.
  - **Rejected:** comparing only the app's version (an out-of-date program would never be reported, and the program
    is what imports, derives and seals); not announcing a program-only gap (the user would not learn that the CLI the
    app runs is out of date); running the upgrade command from the app (a package or checkout upgrade is the user's to
    run, D-1065); telling the CLI to set `update_available` from the app alone (changes the `agentprov-update-check/0.1`
    meaning for every reader, where the document already has `behind`).
- **D-1080 (2026-11-06, the macOS memory watchdog counts compressed and swapped pages: the `libproc` RSS sample is the
  larger of the resident size and `phys_footprint`; a 0.2.0 release CI finding, fixed for 0.2.1 with the user's yes of
  2026-11-06; `host.py`, tests, G.4.11 and G.4.12; class 1).** On GitHub's macos-latest runner (2026-11-05, `ci.yml`
  run 42002097860) `test_sec22_a_job_kind_with_a_declared_cap_runs_past_the_default_cap_and_is_still_bounded` failed:
  the 1.5 GiB hog, whose pages are incompressible and distinct since 8306d770, finished under its 1 GiB kind cap with
  a sampled peak of 1,033,748,480 B. The runner was short of memory, so macOS compressed or swapped the hog's pages
  and the resident size (`proc_pidinfo(PROC_PIDTASKINFO)`) fell below the cap while the process still held them. macOS
  does not enforce `RLIMIT_AS`, so the polled watchdog is its only memory cap (G.4.11), and a job could exceed its cap
  whenever the host was short. This is a gap in the cap, not only a flaky test.
  - **Decision.** The `libproc` sampler returns `max(resident size, phys_footprint)`, with `phys_footprint` from
    `proc_pid_rusage(RUSAGE_INFO_V4)` (the kernel's per-process footprint, which keeps counting compressed pages and
    those swapped out of the compressor; the D-554 admission controller already counts it). Where `proc_pid_rusage`
    is missing or refuses the pid, the resident size alone is used, as before. The capability's value stays
    `libproc`; the watchdog, the per-job peak and the admission fallback all read the one sampler.
  - **Effects.** No AER, SEM or PROV byte changes. `host.py` is in the AER stage's import closure, so the AER stage code
    digest moves (regen-batch row 189). A job's recorded peak can be higher than before on a host short of memory. A
    job that fit under its cap before still fits unless its footprint exceeds the cap.
  - **Rejected:** `phys_footprint` alone (it leaves out shared file-backed pages that the resident size counts, so a
    sample could fall below the old one and let through a job that was stopped before); the kernel's lifetime maximum
    (`ri_lifetime_max_phys_footprint`), because a worker outlives its jobs (D-1068 P1) and an earlier job's peak would
    stop a later one; marking the sec22 case flaky or retrying it (it would hide the gap); a memory pressure check on
    the host (it does not bound one job).
- **D-1081 (2026-11-06, the tier-4 round-trip cache context is the same in a worker and its parent on Windows: the
  Python build is named by `sysconfig.get_platform()`, an unreadable library file makes the context incomplete, and job
  frames carry per-part digests; the cache is used on Windows again; a 0.2.0 release CI finding, fixed for 0.2.1 with
  the user's yes of 2026-11-06; `validate/cache.py`, `cli/checks.py`, tests, MN N.2.5 item 9; class 1).** In the 0.2.0
  Windows CI rounds (2026-11-05, runs 41985115578, 41993437282 and 41995864602, the last with the sharing-violation
  retries of 587db95a in) workers' round trips were not stored (`CacheStats(stored=0, unstorable=3)`) and one staged
  hint in three was refused: the D-550 context of some worker processes differed from the parent's. 0.2.0 shipped with
  the cache off on Windows (9f897315) and its tests skipped there (9f897315, 4a741781).
  - **Cause.** The context's Python part held `platform.machine()`. On Windows, CPython 3.14 answers it with a WMI
    query and, when that query fails, with `PROCESSOR_ARCHITEW6432` or `PROCESSOR_ARCHITECTURE`, neither of which a
    T1 worker's minimal environment carries (G.4.2). A worker whose WMI query failed (they do under load) named the
    machine `""` where its parent named it `AMD64`. Nothing else in the context reads the environment.
  - **Decision 1.** The Python part names the build with `sysconfig.get_platform()` (as D-1064 does for the platform
    label), fixed at build time, the same in every process of one interpreter. Every existing entry becomes a miss
    once.
  - **Decision 2.** A library file that cannot be read, after the sharing-violation retries, no longer contributes the
    digest of a placeholder (`\x00missing`), which looked valid and which no other process computed. The library is
    recorded as unreadable, the context is incomplete (`context_problem`), and that process neither serves nor
    stores an entry: lookups are misses and the counter `context_incomplete` counts refusals; a job with an
    incomplete context uses no hint and says so in its frame.
  - **Decision 3.** A job's frame carries `context_parts`, the digest of each part of its context (`code`, `options`,
    `python`, `vocabulary`, `libraries.<name>`). A frame made under another context than the parent's is counted
    (`context_mismatch`) and not stored, and the command's stderr names the parts that differed and how often, so that
    a host where it still happens can be diagnosed from one run.
  - **Decision 4.** The cache is used on Windows again, and the tests skipped there in 0.2.0 run there. This needed a
    green Windows CI run (no Windows host is available locally): the public trial branch `trial/v0.2.1-windows`
    (`eaa5b8e`, exported from `f5d6b517` onto public `main` `b9b4f0c`; the user's yes of 2026-11-06), `ci.yml` run
    42158076340 (2026-11-06, 03:41-03:55 UTC), passed every job; the four Windows shards ran the cache tests with the
    cache on (only the POSIX-only concurrency case skipped), where shard 3 had failed in all three 0.2.0 runs with
    it on. If a later Windows run fails, the switch is put back and this entry records why.
  - **Effects.** Outcomes, reports, rows and digests of AER, SEM and PROV bytes do not change (the cache is a speed-up
    only, D-550). `validate/cache.py` is in the validation stage's scope, so its code digest moves (regen-batch row
    189); the cache format stays `agentprov-tier4-cache/2`, and entries made before are misses because the context
    moved.
  - **Rejected:** passing `PROCESSOR_ARCHITECTURE` into the worker environment (it would make one call stable and
    leave the context open to the next environment-dependent value); the parent sending its context digest for the
    job to adopt (a job's context must be its own, or a worker with other libraries would serve the parent's
    outcomes); keeping the cache off on Windows (a 0.2.0 stopgap, with validation slower there); hashing RECORD's
    claimed digests instead of the library files (fewer reads, but an edited installed file would be served stale).
- **D-1090 (2026-11-06, Run Live fills the D-725 caps from the quote: `agentprov estimate` suggests caps that leave
  room for what the run reserves, with a margin setting; the user's request and answers of 2026-11-06; CLI, settings,
  GUI, tests and docs; class 0).** An API-endpoint run needs `--max-calls` and `--max-cost-usd` (D-725), and Run Live
  made the user type both before Start; its "Use the quote's upper figure" filled the cost cap with the quote's p90.
  That figure alone often lets no cell start: T0 starts a cell only if the spend so far plus every in-flight cell's
  worst case and its own fit both caps, and one cell's worst case is 48 billed calls (the stock element), 144 (the
  AutoDojo element) or 384 (`gateway_compat`, AU-LIVE-1), each charged at 32,000 input-side and 4,096 output tokens: at
  $3 and $15 per million tokens one `gateway_compat` cell reserves about $60, against quotes of a few dollars.
  - **Decision: the estimate suggests the caps (one rule, the CLI's).** `agentprov estimate` gains `quote.caps`
    (additive): `max_calls` = ⌈`calls_p90` × (1 + m)⌉ + r × B + k, and `max_cost_usd` = `usd_p90` × (1 + m) + (r × B +
    k) × c, rounded up to the cent, where m is the margin, r = min(`--jobs`, the cells due), B the cell's billed-call
    bound, k a preflight probe's billed replies and c one call at the per-call token bound priced at the cap prices
    (`--price-in`/`--price-out` when given, else the price table's, the input side the highest of input, cached input
    and cache write, as Run Live already priced the caps). The p90 figures stay what D-1062 says (the upper figure is
    the sum of per-cell 90th percentiles); the room is what the campaign reserves, so the caps let the run finish if it
    spends what the quote says, and the run can never spend more than them. It also gives `price_in`, `price_out`,
    `margin_pct`, `margin_from` (`setting` or `default`), `calls_basis` `calls_p90`, `cost_basis` `usd_p90`,
    `reserved_cells`, `cell_calls`, `cell_usd`, `probe_calls`, `probe_usd` and `resumed_units` (settled units of the
    corpus, whose spend the caps also count: the text says to add it). The text form prints "Suggested caps:
    --max-calls N --max-cost-usd USD --price-in … --price-out …" with how they were made.
  - **Decision: the bound is the run's own.** `run --dry-run --plan-json` adds `cell_bound: {calls, step_calls,
    call_tokens_in, call_tokens_out}` (additive), computed by the same function that builds the campaign's `Budget`
    (the LLM element's billed replies per step, a defence's declared calls, an Inspect cell's D-740 bound), with or
    without caps, or `cell_bound: {refused}` when it cannot be bounded; a scripted Inspect plan (the estimate's
    stand-in) has none, because its cells are not the model's. `Budget.call_bound()` (public) gives the per-call tokens.
  - **Decision: when there is no suggestion.** `available: false` with a `reason` for a scripted run, a model without
    a price, no cell due, cells resting only on `estimate.default.*` (no priors and no `--stats-corpus` figures; the
    user's choice of 2026-11-06), or no cell bound. All-model priors still suggest caps, and Run Live's caption says
    the figures are not this model's.
  - **Decision: the margin is a setting.** `estimate.caps_margin_pct` (percent, 0 to 1,000; unset: 20, the user's
    choice of 2026-11-06), read by `agentprov estimate` and shown in Settings › Estimate › Run caps as "Margin on the
    quote" (written with `agentprov settings set`). Calls are rounded up to a whole call and USD up to the cent.
  - **Decision: `run` keeps explicit caps** (the user's choice of 2026-11-06). `run` gets no automatic caps mode: the
    caps stay numbers the user saw, which the consent names (D-725). Run Live passes them as `--max-calls` and
    `--max-cost-usd`, and its command card shows the exact values Start passes (D-1060).
  - **Decision: Run Live.** Both cap fields follow `quote.caps` (read defensively; the GUI computes no figure): after
    every new quote, which is asked again on any change to the model, endpoint, benchmark, suites, attacks, task
    selection, repeats, concurrency or prices, a field that follows the quote takes the suggestion, or is cleared
    when there is none (so an API run needs it typed, as before). A value the user types stays, captioned "Your value;
    the quote suggests …", until **Use the quote's figure** beside it (one per cap, replacing "Use the quote's upper
    figure"). Each row's caption says how the figure was made (the p90 calls or the upper cost, the margin, the room,
    local, shipped or both priors, all-model figures when so, and for the cost the prices' source and date) and its
    tooltip gives the numbers, or why there is no suggestion. A cap that follows the quote is left out of the
    estimate's own arguments (it is the estimate's output, and asking again with it would only repeat the quote); a
    typed cap is passed, for the estimate's warnings, and typed prices go with the cost cap (the CLI takes them only
    with `--max-cost-usd`), so the room is priced at them. Since estimate takes no `--preset` and a preset run uses
    `gateway_compat` (D-822), Run Live passes `--llm-element gateway_compat` to the estimate of a preset run that names
    no element.
  - **Rejected:** filling the caps with the quote's figures alone, plus a margin (the user's choice; a run would stop
    at `cap_reached`, or start no cell, whenever the per-cell reservation is larger than what is left); `run
    --caps-from-estimate` (a cap the user never saw, decided inside the run); computing the suggestion in the GUI (a
    second copy of D-725's bound, which would drift from the run's, D-700); a fixed margin (the user asked for a
    setting); refusing to suggest from all-model priors (the user's choice: the caption names them instead); a new
    statistic for the run's total (D-1062's rejection stands).
  - **Downstream effects.** No AER, SEM, PROV, corpus or manifest bytes change and no stage digest moves (`cli/`,
    `estimate/` and `settings.py` are outside every stage scope, as D-1062 records). The estimate document and the
    dry-plan document gain keys only. The GUI's reverse parity (D-700) lists the two reset links; `estimate` keeps its
    options, so forward parity is unchanged.
  - **Tests:** `tests/estimate/test_suggested_caps.py` (the arithmetic, the room, rounding, prices, no suggestion,
    the text line), `tests/estimate/test_estimate.py::test_parse_plan_reads_the_cell_bound`,
    `tests/integration/test_run_plan_json.py` (the bound for the stock element and `gateway_compat`),
    `tests/integration/test_estimate_cmd.py::test_the_quote_suggests_caps_with_room_for_the_reserved_cells` (the
    setting, `--jobs`, the text form, no price), `gui/tests/test_runlive_caps.py` (fill, follow, typed and reset,
    typed prices, no suggestion, the words, the setting, a preset run) and `gui/tests/test_runlive_form.py` (an older
    CLI's quote fills nothing).
  - **Corrected before 0.2.1 (the code review of 2026-11-07).** Two parts of the rule left the caps below what a run
    that spends what the quote says needs. (1) `usd_p90` was the quote's own figure, priced with the cached-input and
    cache-write prices, while the run counts every input-side token at `--price-in` (`Budget.charge`; Anthropic's cache
    write is 1.25 × input, so an input-heavy loop counted about 20 % above the quote): the cost cap's base is now the
    quote's p90 tokens priced at the cap prices (`cap_price`, no discount). (2) k covered one probe, but the run sends
    up to `PROBE_ATTEMPTS` (3) while the verdict is unconfirmed, each charged `step_calls`: k is now 3 ×
    `step_calls`, and `probe_calls`/`probe_usd` give that room. Run Live also plans an API run's estimate with the
    scripted stand-in until both caps are given (a keyed plan without both is refused, D-725/D-702, so no quote came),
    and an Inspect API run's estimate with `--cell-size 1`, the capped run's default (D-740). Class 0.
- **D-1100 (2026-11-06, the `ci.yml` core job's GitHub-hosted legs run on twice as many shards; requested on
  2026-11-06 after the v0.2.0 release; amends D-1020's matrix; workflow, its test and docs only; class 0).** D-1020
  split each GitHub-hosted core leg over several runners (windows-latest over 4, ubuntu-latest over 3,
  ubuntu-24.04-arm and macos-latest over 2: 11 jobs), and its trial run 41289569701 measured a slowest shard of 15.4
  minutes. Each count is now doubled.
  - **Decision: the matrix.** windows-latest over 8 (in both variants, with and without `CI_RUNNER`), ubuntu-latest
    over 6, ubuntu-24.04-arm and macos-latest over 4: 22 GitHub-hosted core jobs, or the self-hosted runner whole plus
    the 8 Windows shards (9 jobs) with `CI_RUNNER` set. The list stays literal JSON in the `include` expression, four
    legs to a line (the `>-` scalar folds the lines into one string, so the expression is the same shape as before).
    Nothing else changes: the units (a file, an `XDIST_GROUPS` group whole), the seconds list
    (`tests/shard_seconds.txt` holds per-file seconds, independent of the count), the fork guard (UC-46), the job ids
    and `tools/ci_local.py`, whose `core` job still runs the suite whole.
  - **Balance.** With the committed seconds list (4,110 s over 635 units) `assign_shards` puts every shard within 1 %
    of the ideal share at 4, 6 and 8 parts (514 s each at 8), and no shard is empty. The heaviest unit,
    `tests/adapters/dtap/test_remap_context_d530.py` (209 s), and the `serial` group (111 s, one worker) stay well under
    a share. The list's drift since 2026-11-01 unbalances shards only, as D-1020 says; regenerate it from the first
    run on the new matrix if a leg's shards drift apart.
  - **Expected cost (not yet measured).** On run 41289569701 each core job spent 0.5 to 1.2 minutes outside its Tests
    step (checkout, uv, Python, the lockfile checks, sync, lint) and, inside it, collected the whole suite before
    deselecting. That fixed part is paid once per job, so doubling the jobs adds about 11 of them: roughly 15 to 20
    runner-minutes on that run's 127, plus each job's billing round-up to a whole minute, while the slowest shard
    should fall from about 15 to about 8 or 9 minutes. The repository that runs CI decides the price: GitHub-hosted
    minutes are free on the public repository and counted, with Windows and macOS at a multiple of Linux, on the
    private development repository. A dispatch now starts 22 core jobs besides the other jobs, so a plan's limit on
    concurrent jobs may queue some of them.
  - **Measured** (dispatch run 42158546503 on the private development repository, main at `f7861c90`, 2026-11-06):
    all 31 jobs passed in 24.7 minutes; the slowest core shard (windows-latest 5/8) took 21.5. The estimate above
    did not hold, for reasons D-1110 takes up: the private repository's runners have 2 vCPUs (macOS 3), half the
    public repository's on which D-1020 was measured; with psutil installed (D-704) `-n auto` counts physical cores, so
    ubuntu-latest and windows-latest ran one xdist worker (ubuntu-24.04-arm 2, macOS 3); at most 20 jobs ran at once,
    so the Windows shards, last in the list, waited up to 9 minutes for a runner; and the Windows shards' test times
    ran from 566 to 1,203 s (mean 787) under the cross-OS seconds list. About 600 billed minutes on the private
    repository (Windows 2x and macOS 10x the Linux rate; about 99 Linux, 234 Windows and 277 macOS); the public
    repository's runs are free.
  - **Tests.** `tests/repo/test_repository_hygiene.py` pins the counts per leg in both variants (besides D-1020's
    1..n check); `tests/unit/testing/test_shards.py`'s end-to-end check reads the widest leg from `ci.yml`, so it now
    collects 8 shards and checks they are disjoint, complete, and keep each file and group whole.
  - **Rejected:** a first job that computes the matrix and hands it on as an output (`fromJSON(needs.x.outputs.y)`):
    one more runner and a serial step before every leg, for a list that changes rarely; generating the legs inside the
    expression (GitHub's expression language has no range or repeat function); keeping D-1020's counts (the slowest
    shard was still about 15 minutes on Windows and macOS).
- **D-1110 (2026-11-06, the `ci.yml` core shards use every logical CPU, Windows goes first, the shards are weighed by
  each OS's own seconds, and the checkout checks run once per leg; the user's request of 2026-11-06 after D-1100's run;
  amends D-1011's worker count and D-1020's seconds list; workflow, `tests/conftest.py`, `tools/slow_tests.py` and their
  tests; class 0).** D-1100's run 42158546503 took 24.7 minutes, its slowest shard 21.5 (D-1100, Measured). Four causes
  were in the logs; each change answers one.
  - **Decision: `-n logical`.** The test step ran `pytest -n auto`, which xdist resolves to
    `psutil.cpu_count(logical=False)` when psutil is importable, as it is in the core environment since D-704. A 2-vCPU
    x64 runner (ubuntu-latest and windows-latest on a private repository) has one physical core, so those shards ran one
    test at a time; the arm64 and macOS runners have one thread a core and were unaffected. `-n logical` counts every
    logical CPU, which is what D-1011 meant by every core of the runner; a 4-vCPU public-repository runner goes from 2
    workers to 4. It changes only how many workers a CI shard starts, never which tests run; `tools/ci_local.py` and the
    queue pass an explicit `-n`.
  - **Decision: Windows first.** With 31 jobs and an account limit of 20 running at once, the jobs that start last are
    the ones GitHub reaches last, and Windows, the slowest leg, was last in the `include` list. It is now first in the
    hosted list (the `CI_RUNNER` list already had it right after the self-hosted job). GitHub does not promise to start
    matrix jobs in list order, so this is a preference, measured on the next run.
  - **Decision: per-OS seconds.** `tests/shard_seconds.txt` keeps its cross-OS mean rows and gains an optional
    `[profile]` section per OS. `ci.yml` sets `AGENTPROV_SHARD_PROFILE` to `${{ runner.os }}-${{ runner.arch }}`
    (`Linux-X64`, `Linux-ARM64`, `macOS-ARM64`, `Windows-X64`); a shard whose profile has a section weighs by it alone
    (a file the section lacks counts by its tests, as before), and any other run by the mean. Every shard of a leg runs
    on the same OS and declares the same profile, so the shards still agree on one split; the variable is taken out of
    the environment with the other two and handed to the xdist workers through `workerinput`. A shard run prints
    `agentprov shard i/n, profile P (weighed by ...)` in its header, and `tools/slow_tests.py --shard-seconds` reads
    each log's profile from that line, writing the mean over all logs as before and each profile's mean over its own
    logs. For that input the test step now runs `--durations=0` (every test timed; the slowest still come first) instead
    of `--durations=30`. The first sections come from the trial run below (Measured).
  - **Decision: the checkout checks once per leg.** The Unicode check (20 to 60 s) and `ruff check` ran in every shard;
    they read the checkout, not the host, so they now run in each leg's shard 1 (`if: matrix.shard == 1`), which keeps
    one run of each per OS.
  - **Expected** (not yet measured): x64 Linux and Windows shards with 2 workers instead of 1, most of the gain where
    tests wait on subprocesses and files; the Windows shards within a few minutes of each other once the list has a
    `Windows-X64` section; about 10 fewer runner-minutes a run from the checks. Measuring runs are best made on the
    public repository, where GitHub-hosted minutes are free and the runners match D-1020's trials.
  - **Measured** (public trial branch `trial/v0.2.1-ci-shards`, `7988b4a0`, exported from `ea676c81` onto public `main`
    `b9b4f0c` with the user's yes of 2026-11-06; run 42163944824, 04:41-04:53 UTC): all 31 jobs passed in 12.4 minutes,
    against D-1100's 24.7 on the private repository and D-1020's trial (slowest shard 15.4). The public runners have 4
    vCPUs (macOS 3): `-n logical` started 4 workers on x64 and arm64, 3 on macOS. The slowest core shard took 7.8
    minutes (windows-latest 1/8 and 4/8); the Tests step of a shard took 213-308 s on ubuntu-latest, 222-309 s on
    ubuntu-24.04-arm, 340-449 s on macOS and 240-421 s on Windows (mean 324), still weighed by the cross-OS mean. The
    20-job limit held here too, and GitHub did not keep the list order: four Windows shards, among them the two slowest,
    started 3.8 to 4.6 minutes in, so the run is about that wait plus the slowest shard. The 22 core jobs used 126
    runner-minutes (137 rounded up per job), free on the public repository. `tests/shard_seconds.txt` is regenerated
    from this run's 22 `--durations=0` logs: the mean over 711 files (5,393 s) and one section per profile (Linux-ARM64
    3,389 s, Linux-X64 4,701 s, macOS-ARM64 4,110 s, Windows-X64 8,232 s); with it `assign_shards` puts each leg's
    shards within 1 % of each other in test seconds (Windows 1,029 s each, about 4.3 minutes on 4 workers). The heaviest
    unit, `tests/adapters/dtap/test_remap_context_d530.py` (524 s on Windows), is five tests of about 100 s that the
    shard's workers share. Still open: the queueing (fewer, longer jobs, or the self-hosted runner taking the Linux and
    macOS legs, would keep the run under the limit).
  - **Tests.** `tests/unit/testing/test_shards.py`: the profile is optional and a malformed one refused; a section
    replaces the mean for its profile only; the generator writes each named profile beside the mean and conftest reads
    the file back unchanged; a shard run prints the header line the generator reads; no test sees any of the three
    variables. `tests/repo/test_repository_hygiene.py` pins Windows first, the profile variable, `-n logical`,
    `--durations=0` and the two checks' `if`.
  - **Rejected:** `PYTEST_XDIST_AUTO_NUM_WORKERS` or a fixed `-n 2` (both hard-code a count that `logical` reads from
    the runner); oversubscribing (`-n 4` on 2 vCPUs: more memory on small runners, and the pool groups already start
    worker pools of their own; to try only if `logical` leaves the CPUs idle); deriving the profile inside conftest from
    `sys.platform` and the machine (CI names the profile once, from the runner it got, and a local run never weighs by a
    CI profile); one seconds file per OS (four generated files for one table); running the checkout checks in one job
    for the whole run (a check could differ on Windows' checkout, so one per OS is kept).
- **D-1120 (2026-11-06, Run Live configures and starts an Inspect task: AgentHarm from the GUI, the way the
  AgentDojo-family backends are; requested 2026-11-06; GUI `live/plan.py`, `live/inspectplan.py`, `ui/runlive.py`,
  `ui/forms.py`, a shipped Inspect dev script, tests and guide chapter 8; class 0).** `agentprov run agentharm
  --catalogue` answers `agentprov-inspect-catalogue/0.1` (D-663), which Run Live's parser did not read, so choosing
  `agentharm` showed "catalogue unusable" and no way to plan; the Inspect options (`--task`, `--samples`, the limits,
  `--judge`) were free-text rows under Advanced, with `--task-param` typed by hand.
  - **Decision: the Inspect catalogue is parsed like the AgentDojo one.** `parse_inspect_catalogue` (and
    `parse_any_catalogue`, dispatching on `format`) rebuilds typed tasks, parameters (type `str`, `int` or `bool|null`,
    default, choices, bounds), splits with their sample counts, judge roles and the task's fixed settings: bounded
    lists, names that are labels (the CLI's own patterns in `cli/live/inspect_catalogue.py`, mirrored and pinned by a
    test, D-391), whole numbers, no duplicates, unknown members dropped; a judge role must be one `--judge ROLE=MODEL`
    takes. Every name is shown through `text.line`. A catalogue of the other kind than the backend's id (`inspect-` or
    not, the CLI's rule) is unusable, so nothing is launched for it.
  - **Decision: an Inspect backend has its own rows; the AgentDojo-only rows are hidden.** *Inspect task* (the task,
    its fixed settings as facts), *Task parameters* (one row per declared parameter: a menu for choices and for
    true / false / not set, a whole number within its bounds, text otherwise), *Samples and limits* (the first N of the
    split, whose size the caption gives, or ids; the three per-sample limits, required, D-667), *Judges* (one row per
    role, blank = the agent's model, the scorer's default offered) and a closed line with epochs, concurrent model
    calls and cell size. The benchmark version, suites, attacks, benign cells, user and injection tasks and `--defence`
    are hidden and never reach the argv (rule 3; the CLI refuses them for an Inspect plan). The Inspect fields leave
    *Other run options*.
  - **Decision: one argv.** The rows fill `RunSettings.extra`, and the existing builder (`jobs.commands.build_spec`)
    makes the command card, the estimate and Start from it, as for every run. A parameter at its catalogue default is
    left out; any other is `--task-param NAME=VALUE`, written as the CLI reads it (a TOML scalar, else the text), so a
    string that would read as a boolean, number or date is quoted. A real run's blank judges take the agent's model;
    a scripted run's judges take the scripted agent's label (`scripted-fake`, the CLI's). The test runs the CLI's own
    parser and `_inspect_document` on the argv in a child interpreter.
  - **Decision: the checks say what the CLI and worker would refuse, first.** Start and the estimate wait until a task,
    the samples and all three limits are given; a sample count above the split's size, malformed ids, an Anthropic
    endpoint (D-741) and, under the caps, a judge on another model than the agent's (D-740) block Start with the
    reason. Before-you-start and the caps (D-725, D-1090) work as for any backend.
  - **Decision: a combined dev script for scripted Inspect runs.** The worker refuses scripted judges from a plain
    script (`scripted_steps`), so the shipped AgentDojo dev script cannot run an Inspect cell. The app ships
    `scripted-dev-inspect.json` (`{"agent": [...], "judges": {"refusal_judge": [...], "semantic_judge": [...]}}`, 100
    agent replies and 400 per judge), which *Script* switches to while the backend is an Inspect one and back after;
    a script the user chose is kept. A cell that would need more than 100 samples × epochs from it blocks Start.
  - **Rejected:** keeping the Inspect options as free text under Advanced (the user would type `--task-param` values,
    judge roles and sample selections the catalogue already lists); passing every parameter, defaults included (an
    option at its default is left out everywhere else); a switch for `bool|null` (it cannot say "not set", the
    default); judges defaulted to the scorer's own model (under the caps the CLI refuses any judge model other than
    the agent's, D-740); a generated script per run (the dev script is a test fixture, the corpus is `test_only`).
  - **Downstream effects.** None outside the GUI: no CLI option, AER, SEM, PROV, corpus or manifest byte changes and no
    stage digest moves. Forward parity is unchanged (every Inspect option still has a control); reverse parity
    (D-700) maps the new inputs, with `param_widgets.*` and `judge_inputs.*` for the rows built per task.
  - **Not verified here:** a scripted Inspect cell run end to end from the app (only `--catalogue`, `--dry-run
    --plan-json` and `estimate` were run against `inspect-agentharm-f698b6d1`), and a real-model run (none was
    started).
  - **Tests:** `gui/tests/test_runlive_inspect.py` (parsing, a hostile catalogue, the pinned CLI rules, the dev script,
    `--task-param` quoting, the rows and what is hidden, the scripted and real argv through the CLI's parser and plan
    builder, ids and defaults, judges under the caps, the dev script's capacity, a mismatched catalogue, the AgentDojo
    path afterwards, tooltips for both transports) and `gui/tests/test_reverse_parity.py` (an AgentHarm walk).
- **D-1130 (2026-11-06, the update brings the whole software up to date: the bundle is also the `agentprov` program,
  a package install is upgraded from the release's own verified wheels, a clean checkout on `main` is fast-forwarded,
  all in one confirmed flow; amends D-1065 and D-1070; the user's approved plan of 2026-11-06, for 0.2.1 at the user's
  request ("this needs to go in 0.2.1"), and their choice that the update also pulls the checkout; CLI `update`, new
  `update/package.py`, `update/checkout.py`, `cli/frozen.py`, the bundle's entry point and spec, GUI, tests and docs;
  class 0).** D-1065 replaced only the app's folder; "the command-line program is never replaced": without `--bundle`,
  `update install` printed an upgrade command. The app runs its CLI through `CliLocator` (the checkout's `.venv`, else
  an installed `agentprov`), and the bundle carried a copy of the core it could not run as a CLI, so an app update left
  the program behind (the stale `.venv` of D-1070 was one case of it).
  - **Decision: the bundle is its own `agentprov`.** The bundle's one executable answers, before Qt is imported
    (`gui/packaging/entry.py` → `agentprov.cli.frozen.dispatch`): `AgentPROV --cli ARGS` (= `agentprov ARGS`), the
    argv the core itself starts with `sys.executable` (`-I [-B] -m MODULE` for exactly `agentprov`,
    `agentprov.jobs.supervisor`, `agentprov.worker`, `agentprov.keys.helper` and `agentprov.update.apply`; a test
    scans the core for `-m agentprov…` argv and fails on a module the bundle does not answer), and `--keychain-helper`.
    Any other module, a script path or `-c` is refused (exit 2): the bundle is not a general interpreter, so
    `agentprov.host`'s `RLIMIT_AS` probe (`-c`) is "not decided" there and the worker pool falls back as on a host
    where the probe cannot run. `multiprocessing.freeze_support()` runs first (the priors builder's pool). The spec
    collects every core module, `agentprov_capture`, keyring's backends and rdflib's plugins; not the `render`,
    `shacl` and `live` extras or `agentprov-zenodo`. `CliLocator` falls back to it when no checkout is set and no
    installed `agentprov` is found, and Settings › General's new **agentprov to run** (`paths/cli_choice`:
    Automatic, or The app's own) can choose it always; it is then updated with the app. `update install` run by it
    reports the kind `bundle`. **What still needs a checkout:** live runs (`run`, `backends`, `migrate` find
    `backends/` from a checkout; Run Live now says so before a start when the CLI is the app's own), the job queue
    (`--queue-cpu`, `tools/suite_queue.py`), the checkout's tools (`jobs start --tool`), the Zenodo uploader, and
    `render` (Graphviz and the extra). When the bundle's own CLI swaps the bundle it runs from, everything used after
    the swap is imported before it (a module first imported afterwards would come from the new bundle's files), and on
    Windows the helper runs from a copy of the new bundle in `.AgentPROV-update-helper/` beside the app, since a
    helper running from the folder it renames could never rename it (a leftover copy with its marker is removed at the
    next install; a folder without it is refused). The bundle build's smoke step checks `--cli --version`, `-I -m
    agentprov --version` (the bundled core's version) and that `--cli update install` names the kind `bundle`. On
    Windows the bundle is a GUI-subsystem executable, so for `--cli` started from a console it attaches to the parent
    console and reopens only the streams Python has none of (`AttachConsole(ATTACH_PARENT_PROCESS)`, `CONOUT$`,
    `CONIN$`); a pipe from the app or a job is kept. The Windows paths are untested by the project's tests and the
    release notes say so.
  - **Decision: a package install from the release's own wheels.** `agentprov update download --package
    --allow-network` (R2) stages in `$AGENTPROV_HOME/update/staging/package/` (or `--dir`), in this order:
    `SHA256SUMS` and `SHA256SUMS.sig`, verified by D-1065's rule (a listed key requires a valid signature); then the
    release's `agentprov_capture-X-py3-none-any.whl`, `agentprov-X-…whl` and, when installed here,
    `agentprov_zenodo-X-…whl`, each with the listed size (at most 64 MiB) and sha256; then each wheel read, never
    unpacked: at most 10,000 members, no absolute, `..`, backslash or drive name, no encrypted member, and one
    `<dist>-X.dist-info/METADATA` naming that distribution and version. A failure removes what was fetched. Its
    document (`agentprov-update-download/0.1`, `kind: package`) also says what installing would do: `install_kind`,
    `from_version`, `to_version`, `parts`, `installer`, `installer_argv`, `installable`, `problems`,
    `keeps_previous: false`, `restore_command`. `agentprov update install --package --confirm` (R2; exit 4 without
    `--confirm`) verifies every staged file again (a changed wheel or list is refused), refuses a downgrade (exit 4),
    reports the same version as current, and runs the program's own installer on exactly those files with no
    resolver and no index: `pip` → `<its interpreter> -m pip install --no-deps --no-index --disable-pip-version-check
    --no-input WHEELS` (a venv without pip: `uv pip install --python <it> --no-deps --no-index`); `uv-tool` → `uv pip
    install --python <its interpreter> --no-deps --no-index WHEELS`; `pipx` → `pipx runpip <venv> install --no-deps
    --no-index …`; the installer's environment drops `PIP_*`, `UV_*`, `PYTHON*`, `VIRTUAL_ENV`, `CONDA_*`. Because
    nothing is resolved, it refuses (exit 4, `update.package.dependencies`, with the ordinary upgrade command) a
    release whose wheels need anything the installed version did not declare: every non-sibling requirement must
    equal, after normalising, one the installed distribution already has (so it is already satisfied), and every
    sibling requirement must be `==X`. Afterwards the installed versions are read again and must be the release's
